source.title: Identifying and removing widespread signal deflections from fMRI data: Rethinking the global signal regression problem

confidence_rationale: Supports SD-079's premise on strong empirical footing -- across three independent datasets plus 47 task contrasts from the Human Connectome Project, removing a shared widespread component demonstrably improves anatomical specificity and reduces spurious structure. But the paper's central result is that a SINGLE global mean estimate captures only one kind of widespread coherent structure, and that an iterative cluster-based estimator (DiCER) removes more of it and better preserves genuine task-related structure. SD-079 uses a single scalar-alpha EMA mean vector, which is the class of estimator this paper finds incomplete. Confidence 0.55 because mapping fidelity is the weakest of the four entries in this pull: the evidence is about the sufficiency of an estimator in a spatiotemporal imaging pipeline, and the argument that it generalises to an online latent baseline is structural rather than demonstrated.
failure_signatures: A single global-mean estimate is only effective against specific kinds of widespread coherent structure. The paper reordered carpet plots to expose cluster structure and found a greater diversity of widespread signal deflections than previously recognised, varying across time and across participants, of which global signal regression removes only some -- so 'the common mode has been subtracted' does not entail 'the common mode has been removed'.

Removal of a shared component can distort between-group comparisons of the resulting connectivity measures. The REE analogue is arm-vs-arm comparison: an ON arm and an OFF arm differing in whether centering is applied are not merely differing in one term, since centering alters the distribution of every downstream match, and a between-arm delta can therefore reflect the estimator rather than the mechanism under test.

The common mode is not necessarily stationary in form. The paper reports that the precise form of widespread deflections varies across time and participants, so an estimator tuned on one regime can under-remove in another -- the direct analogue of SD-079's own finding that alpha 0.02 lags a drifting z_goal (spread 0.0942 / 0.1508 / 0.3319 across seeds 101/202/303) while 0.05 tracks it.

mapping.source_claim_statement: Global signal regression -- removal of the mean signal averaged over the entire brain -- improves quality-control metrics, enhances the anatomical specificity of functional-connectivity patterns and can increase behaviourally-explained variance, but also alters the distribution of regional correlations, can induce artefactual anticorrelations, may remove real neural signal, and can distort case-control comparisons. Reordering carpet plots to emphasise cluster structure reveals a greater diversity of spatially widespread signal deflections than previously thought; their precise form varies across time and participants, and global signal regression is effective at removing only specific kinds. An iterative alternative, Diffuse Cluster Estimation and Regression (DiCER), which identifies representative signals associated with large clusters of coherent voxels, removes diverse widespread deflections more effectively, reduces correlations between functional connectivity and head motion, reduces inter-individual variability in global correlation structure, and better preserves the expected spatial structure of task-related activation across 47 contrasts from 7 Human Connectome Project tasks.
mapping.ree_translation: SD-079's baseline is a single EMA-estimated mean vector, updated at one fixed rate (goal_cue_baseline_alpha, default 0.05), shared between AnchorSet and GhostGoalBank, and subtracted from z_goal before every goal_match. This paper is the closest available external test of whether a single mean estimate is the RIGHT estimator for a common mode, as distinct from whether common-mode removal is the right operation. Its answer is a qualified no: the operation is correct and beneficial, but one global mean captures only part of the widespread coherent structure present, and a richer estimator recovers more while doing less collateral damage to genuine structure. Applied to SD-079, this predicts that centered z_goal will retain residual shared structure that the EMA baseline does not reach, and that the residual will be non-stationary in form rather than merely in magnitude. SD-079 has already met the magnitude version of this problem and solved it empirically -- alpha 0.02 lags a drifting z_goal while 0.05 tracks it -- which is evidence the team is on the correct side of the estimator question, but the paper's point is about the estimator's FORM (a single mean direction) and no alpha choice addresses that.
mapping.mapping_caveat: This is the weakest-fidelity entry in this pull and should be cited as suggestive, not decisive. Three gaps. (1) The paper's evidence for estimator insufficiency is spatial: carpet plots reordered to expose voxel clusters, and structure that is widespread across ANATOMY. REE's z_goal has no spatial organisation and no notion of a 'cluster of coherent voxels', so the specific diagnostic that motivated DiCER cannot be run on it and the argument that an analogous residual exists is structural inference, not measurement. (2) DiCER's advantages are measured against fMRI-specific criteria -- head-motion correlation, inter-individual variability, canonical network recovery, task-activation preservation -- none of which has a REE counterpart, so 'better' here is not shown to be better for anything REE cares about. (3) The paper concerns an offline, whole-session estimator with access to all timepoints; SD-079's baseline is causal and online. An offline estimator's superiority does not establish that a richer online estimator is achievable at acceptable cost. The honest use of this entry is as a named open question -- is one mean direction enough for z_goal? -- rather than as a defect finding against the landed fix, which V3-EXQ-807 and V3-EXQ-823 both measured as working.
mapping.source_context: Human resting-state fMRI across three independent datasets, plus task fMRI from the Human Connectome Project spanning 47 contrasts across 7 tasks; offline preprocessing pipeline comparison; code publicly released.

confidence_components.notes: source_quality high: NeuroImage, three independent replication datasets plus a large public task corpus, a proposed method evaluated against multiple orthogonal criteria rather than one favourable metric, open code. mapping_fidelity 0.50 is the binding constraint and is deliberately low -- the paper's core evidence depends on spatial cluster structure that has no analogue in a latent vector, so the transfer of its conclusion rests on an argument rather than a measurement. transfer_risk 0.55 for the same reason, compounded by the offline-versus-online distinction. Aggregate 0.55, close to mapping_fidelity rather than to source_quality, because for a design_decision claim a well-executed study of a differently-shaped system is worth about what its mapping is worth.
